claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed, thin, continuous iron-oxide film.
The native film on Q235 consists of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
The native iron-oxide film acts as a protective diffusion barrier during high-temperature salt exposure.
Disrupting the native oxide film will accelerate corrosion of Q235 steel.
Controlled pre-oxidation will produce a thicker or more adherent oxide film.
Pre-oxidized Q235 will have better corrosion resistance than untreated Q235.
Oxide-scale integrity, adherence, and microstructural quality govern the protection of Q235 steel.
An intact oxide film limits inward diffusion of molten-salt constituents.
An intact oxide film limits outward diffusion of iron ions.
Restricting inward corrosive-species transport and outward iron transport slows corrosion.
Removing or disrupting the oxide exposes the underlying metal and thereby accelerates mass loss and degradation.
Molten-salt exposure at approximately 700 °C can produce corrosion-related mass change and degradation.
At 700 °C, intact or pre-oxidized Q235 samples will show lower mass loss than oxide-disrupted samples.
At 700 °C, intact or pre-oxidized Q235 samples will show lower pit density than oxide-disrupted samples.
At 700 °C, intact or pre-oxidized Q235 samples will show less surface degradation than oxide-disrupted samples.
Differences among the surface-treatment groups will be minimal at room temperature because reaction kinetics are slower.
The oxide film is less important under room-temperature corrosion conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when localized pitting caused by aggressive ions operates independently of oxide-film integrity.
Variations in minor alloying elements or environmental contaminants may alter oxide-film effects and corrosion kinetics.
